18   1    Introduction
19   Evaluating a language model means running it on dozens to hundreds of benchmarks, each costing
20   compute and effort. Public leaderboards meanwhile hold a history matrix of the scores of M earlier
21   models on N benchmarks. An evaluator facing a new model can afford only k ≪ N runs and wants
22   its scores on the other benchmarks. We ask three questions: which k benchmarks to run, how well the
23   rest can then be inferred, and how large k must be.
24   Earlier work, which we survey in Section 2, reduces the number of items inside one benchmark or
25   completes matrices whose observed cells are random. Choosing the k benchmarks is a design problem,
26   to be tested on a model family absent from the history and on models newer and stronger than it;
27   leave-one-model-out evaluation leaves near-identical siblings in the history and makes prediction
28   look easier than it is.
29   We study the problem with a protocol that holds out whole model families (and, separately, later
30   release dates), fits everything on the training models before selecting benchmarks, and compares
31   selectors and predictors on identical targets with family-clustered, paired uncertainty (Section 3).
32   The method is a known toolkit applied to a new matrix: a factor model with diagonal noise fitted to
33   the history, Gaussian conditioning to predict the unrun benchmarks, and greedy Bayesian A-optimal

## M1 (sparse leaderboard matrix): answered
The paper now runs the protocol on MTEB matrices with their real missing cells (21-70 % observed, English and all tasks; Section 6.6, Table 3, Appendix C.2, Fig. 9, Table 11) and says in Section 7 which conditions remain open (no density below 21 %, identity transform only, models with fewer than 30 cells untested).

- The protocol (training-only fits, same candidates and targets for both selectors, LOBO analogue as the better of two predictors, closure above 1 possible) is what the code does, and the text says so.

## Earlier `may` findings
Abstract states that the 10 % margin is met on one pool of three; closure and A-optimal are defined in the abstract; the pre-specification record is named (released code, Appendix D); the checklist agrees with the paper (limitations, 2-22 CPU minutes).

- Dense-pool results remain on selected pools and on embedding / MMLU data; the paper says so in the abstract, Section 6.1 and Section 7.
- The pre-specified hypotheses are reported as they fell: H1 fails, H2 on one pool of three, H4 fails; k* is given with intervals and a bias warning.

shown.message:
I approved `paper-repo`#7 (`main` into `final`) at head `1069b15`. The review is posted on the PR, so the merge into `final` can go ahead.

- **M1 is answered.** The paper now runs the protocol on MTEB matrices with their real missing cells (21–70% observed, English and all tasks). It states what is still open: no density below 21%, identity transform only, and models with fewer than 30 observed cells untested.
- **The numbers match.** Table 3's gaps, intervals, closure at k=3 and k\* with censoring all match `results/sparse_*.csv`. The protocol in `code/bmk/sparse.py` is what the text describes.
- **The earlier minor findings are fixed:**
  - The abstract now says the 10% margin is met on one pool of three.
  - The abstract defines closure and A-optimal.
  - The paper says where the pre-specification is recorded.
  - The checklist agrees with the paper.
- **A note that does not hold the version back:** the factor-model numbers on the "All tasks 50%" row are unstable. Random selection there has closure -0.08, and the gap interval is [-0.629, -0.092]. The paper uses the pairwise-correlation predictor as the headline and says so.

The review record is `reviews/paper-repo-7-final-1069b15.md` in my repository.
